input:
the lifetime figures reported for the benchmark material conflict, largely because the two groups end the test at different points in the material's decline. One group reports the service time at which capacity first falls below the level its separation needs, while the other reports the time at which half the fresh capacity remains. The second endpoint is naturally reached later in the life of the same sample, and a material that fails the first group's test early can still post the longer figure under the second group's endpoint. The reported order of the two materials in each study therefore follows the endpoint as much as the material, and the studies broadly agree once each figure is read against its own endpoint.
The conditions differ in a second way as well. One group regenerates fully between exposures, so that each measurement starts from the same state; the other regenerates on the application's schedule, and incomplete regeneration accumulates across the test. IAST is used by both groups to correct the mixed-gas capacities, and the correction does not account for the accumulated state, so the second group's later figures carry a decline that the correction leaves in the capacity rather than in the model. On the application's duty — regeneration on the application's schedule, and the end of life set by the capacity the separation needs — the second group's value is the one this review rests on, because its test reproduces the accumulation the application imposes. The preference rests on that match of duty: on a duty with full regeneration between exposures, the first group's value would be the applicable one, and neither figure transfers cleanly across the two duties
